title: LNER's on-train AIVR camera AI flags a minor track fault near Retford a week after a driver-reported defect cost 10,000 delay minutes; overnight repair, zero delay minutes
summary: LNER reports that AIVR’s underbody cameras detected a minor Retford fault that engineers repaired overnight without passenger delays. The separate Cambridgeshire disruption is not delay saved.
account: New Civil Engineer's Tom Pashby reported on 6 Jul 2026. His story was about the system flagging a snake as a track defect on 3 July. LNER runs the Pantograph Damage Assessment System (PANDAS) and One Big Circle's Automated Intelligent Video Review (AIVR) on a number of its trains. They assess overhead line equipment and track and report potential damage to Network Rail. The article reproduces LNER's 9 April 2026 announcement. In January 2026 a train driver in Cambridgeshire reported a track defect. It caused over 10,000 delay minutes, multiple cancellations and a full day of disruption. A week later the AIVR system identified a minor fault near Retford with the potential to become a larger issue. Engineers carried out an overnight repair with no delay to passengers and zero delay minutes. An LNER spokesperson said the information is fed back to Network Rail to target areas for attention. A Network Rail spokesperson said the snake would be raised automatically as standard practice. LNER’s original April 9 announcement describes underbody line-scanning cameras on two bi-mode Azuma trains. The exact day of the Retford detection is not given. The 10,000 delay minutes concern the separate Cambridgeshire event, not measured delays saved at Retford.
purpose: AIVR is built to capture and analyze front-of-train video with machine learning. The aim is to find and fix track and lineside defects before they cause disruption.
system: Automated Intelligent Video Review (AIVR), using underbody line-scanning cameras on two LNER bi-mode Azuma trains
deployer: LNER (on-train cameras), with findings passed to Network Rail

ratings.reason: An overnight planned repair with zero delay minutes. The comparison is a defect the same month that cost over 10,000 delay minutes and a day of disruption.
Passengers were spared delay from this fault. The scale of avoided disruption is not quantified.

ai_role.statement: AIVR's analysis raised the fault report that Network Rail engineers acted on. No human had reported it. Whether the minor fault would have escalated is LNER's claim. Detection rates and false-positive rates are not published.

fields.account: New Civil Engineer's Tom Pashby reported on 6 Jul 2026. His story was about the system flagging a snake as a track defect on 3 July. LNER runs the Pantograph Damage Assessment System (PANDAS) and One Big Circle's Automated Intelligent Video Review (AIVR) on a number of its trains. They assess overhead line equipment and track and report potential damage to Network Rail. The article reproduces LNER's 9 April 2026 announcement. In January 2026 a train driver in Cambridgeshire reported a track defect. It caused over 10,000 delay minutes, multiple cancellations and a full day of disruption. A week later the AIVR system identified a minor fault near Retford with the potential to become a larger issue. Engineers carried out an overnight repair with no delay to passengers and zero delay minutes. An LNER spokesperson said the information is fed back to Network Rail to target areas for attention. A Network Rail spokesperson said the snake would be raised automatically as standard practice. LNER’s original April 9 announcement describes underbody line-scanning cameras on two bi-mode Azuma trains. The exact day of the Retford detection is not given. The 10,000 delay minutes concern the separate Cambridgeshire event, not measured delays saved at Retford.
